query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion of the high-density refractory elements (Hf, Ta, W) in as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with lower-density refractory elements (specifically V or Nb) and/or light elements (Al, Ti) to form a dual-phase BCC/B2 or BCC/L12 microstructure will reduce the alloy density while maintaining or enhancing high-temperature strength through precipitation hardening and solid solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3, exhibiting high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to ~1000 °C) but limited by high density.
generation.intervention: Partial substitution of Hf and Ta with lower-density refractory elements (e.g., V, Nb) and/or addition of light elements (Al, Ti) to create a modified composition (e.g., HfMoNbTiZr or HfMoTaTiZr-xAl), followed by controlled heat treatment to induce precipitation of ordered phases (B2 or L12) within a BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Vacuum arc melting or induction melting followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C and 207 MPa for 1 h, and vacuum annealing at 1200 °C for 24 h to stabilize the microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a BCC solid solution matrix reinforced by coherent or semi-coherent ordered precipitates (B2 or L12) with high anti-phase boundary energy, similar to the 'high entropy superalloy' (HESA) concept.
generation.mechanism: Density reduction is achieved by replacing heavy atoms (Hf, Ta) with lighter ones (V, Nb, Al) while maintaining the refractory nature of the alloy. High-temperature strength is preserved or enhanced via precipitation strengthening (from ordered phases) and solid solution strengthening, leveraging the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix and high anti-phase boundary energy of the precipitates, as observed in HESAs and refractory HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a density reduction of at least 5-10% (targeting <9.5 g cm−3) compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, while maintaining yield strength >400 MPa at 1000 °C and exhibiting superior creep resistance comparable to Ni-based superalloys.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with density 10.21 g cm−3 and high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Applicable for temperatures from room temperature up to 1000 °C; loading conditions include tensile and creep loading; the intervention is limited to compositions where the BCC matrix remains stable and does not form brittle intermetallics that compromise ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition window for optimal density reduction without compromising high-temperature ductility or inducing phase instability is uncertain; the long-term stability of the precipitates at temperatures >1000 °C requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HfMoTaTiZr-based alloys with incremental substitution of Hf/Ta by V/Nb/Al (e.g., HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr-5Al, HfMoTaTiZr-10Al). Process all samples via vacuum arc melting, HIP, and annealing. Measure density, tensile strength, and creep resistance at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Tensile yield strength at room temperature and 1000 °C
Creep strain rate at 1000 °C under 200 MPa
Microstructural analysis (XRD, SEM, TEM) to confirm phase constitution and precipitate stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any modified alloy exhibits a density reduction <5% while maintaining strength >400 MPa at 1000 °C, or if the strength drops below 300 MPa at 1000 °C despite density reduction, the hypothesis is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties
